description: SUNVI is a multidisciplinary team from Benin passionate about science, technology, space exploration, AI, and innovation. Our skills include energy engineering, programming, artificial intelligence, electronics, and applied sciences. We value creativity, teamwork, and problem-solving. We welcome motivated participants with skills in software development, data science, astronomy, robotics, UI/UX design, and communication. Join us to turn ideas into impactful solutions!
summary: Earthrise Atlas helps anyone choose where, and when, to land near the Moon's south pole. At the pole the Sun skims the horizon and the Earth hides behind mountains for days, so a site that looks perfect one week can leave a lander without power or radio the next. Pick a site and a date: Earthrise Atlas uses NASA's lunar relief data and the real horizon around the site to show, hour by hour, when the Sun lights the solar panels and when the Earth is in view for direct radio contact. It turns this into four key figures and a clear verdict ("feasible" or not) for a small solar lander. We built it because planning a polar landing today needs expert tools and specialist data, and we wanted mission planners, students and the curious public to understand the south pole and plan a landing in minutes.
details:
Live website: https://earthrise-atlas.vercel.app

Source code: https://github.com/Sunvi-children-of-the-stars/Earthrise-Atlas

WHAT IT DOES

Earthrise Atlas is a free website (English and French) for comparing lunar south pole landing sites and dates. It has five parts:

- Story: a six-chapter introduction to the south pole (why the Sun never sets on some ridges, why the Earth disappears for days, how the Moon differs from home), computed on a real lunar day.

- Atlas: a real LROC photo of the south pole with 14 reference sites (Artemis III candidate regions, IM-1, IM-2, Chandrayaan-3, Chang'e-6 and other historic landing sites). Any point can be tried by clicking the map or typing coordinates.

- Play: choose a site, a start date and a duration. You get four key figures (sunlight, Earth in view, Earth or relay contact, mission verdict) and four views: the sky panorama with the Sun and Earth moving above the real horizon, a timeline of light and radio windows, a 3D view of 20 x 20 km of real terrain lit by the Sun with cast shadows, and the site details. If the mission slips by a month, Earthrise Atlas compares both dates and searches for better spots within 10 km. Each scenario can be shared as a link or downloaded as a one-page PDF mission sheet.

- Mission Lab: for advanced users. It ranks safe zones in 9 polar regions at 200 m resolution, with profiles such as "crewed Artemis III" (slope, length of nights, sunlight, Earth visibility, distance to permanently shadowed regions, Diviner temperatures), shows the best landing dates on a site by lunar-month calendar, computes an energy and radio budget (battery, solar panels, LRO relay and model Gateway and Queqiao-2 orbits), and compares sites side by side.

- Method: data sources, validation results and the team.

HOW IT WORKS

For each site we compute the horizon mask: the elevation of the surrounding terrain in every direction, from the LOLA 20 m elevation models, including the curvature of the Moon. The Sun and Earth positions come from a JPL Horizons table (2026 to 2030). A body is visible when it is above the horizon mask; the Sun is treated as a disk, so partial sunlight is counted. From this we get light and radio windows, the longest night, the longest blackout and the verdict. Heavy pre-computations (regional horizon maps, LROC mosaic) ran in the cloud on Modal; everything else runs in the visitor's browser, with no server, so the site is fast and free to host.

VALIDATION

- Sun and Earth positions match JPL Horizons within 0.003 degrees.

- Our permanently shadowed regions overlap the official LOLA maps with an IoU of 0.80 to 0.93, and our average illumination differs by 2.1 to 2.5 percentage points (RMS).

- Taking lunar curvature into account reduces the illumination error from 11 to 3.1 points.

- 105 automated tests check the calculations.

BENEFITS

- Mission teams can screen sites and dates in seconds, before running detailed studies.

- Students and the public can see why the south pole is such a hard and exciting place to land, and why "Earthrise" matters for radio contact.

- Everything is open: the data, the code and the results.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

We want Earthrise Atlas to become an open companion for the Artemis era: a place where anyone can check a landing site, understand the trade-offs between light, radio and terrain, and share a scenario with one link.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Three.js (3D view), Web Workers, jsPDF and html-to-image (PDF sheet), Vitest (tests); Python with NumPy, tifffile and imagecodecs (data processing); Modal (cloud computing); Vercel (hosting); ffmpeg (demo video).
